chapters.title: Intent to Kill
chapters.html:
In many ways, the fight against Nikador is the fight that Mydei has been preparing for his entire life.

Despite his bravado, he understands Phainon’s hesitation. The towering figure before them is the most feared god in their world, the embodiment of Strife itself. Killing any titan is an intimidating prospect; killing Nikador, then, is a trulyoverwhelming one. But Mydei has never had the luxury of hesitation. And so, he fights.

It is a good battle. Despite her strange choice of weapon, Stelle is surprisingly strong. She’s clever and strategic, too, despite how odd her words can be. Phainon is powerful and precise, a trained swordsman who understands Mydei’s combat style. They complement each other well, covering for each other’s weaknesses and able to predict where the other will be. And if Phainon doesn’t like the risky attacks he sometimes prefers… well, the battle is too fast-paced to linger on the disapproving frown of the other Chrysos Heir.

Finally, with a crushing blow from Mydei’s fist, Nikador, Titan of Strife, shudders and collapses to the ground. The god lies defeated, their mechanical body reduced to nothing more than a heap of scrap. The sounds of combat recede, and a loaded, expectant silence hangs in the air.

There is a moment when Mydei thinks—hopes, perhaps—that the battle is truly won. Next to him, Phainon exhales loudly, undoubtedly preparing to give some foolish speech. Mydei smirks. But his expression immediately turns to a grimacewhen he sees a golden light emanate from the titan’s corpse, and the pieces of their body start to move.

Within seconds, Nikador glows a blinding gold. The light fades, leaving behind theirreformed body.

“Immortal wretch… how amusing.” There’s a certain dark humor to it. Of course his god, corrupted as they are, shares his curse.

The Blade of Fury soars up to the dark sky. The titan’s massive weapon hangs overhead menacingly, poised to fall at any moment. The threat to Okhema is undeniable.

As always, Phainon is far more vocal than he needs to be. "The souls of war are amassing in the skies above Kremnos... surging toward the Blade of Fury! They have no intention of winning the fight. Instead, they're using death after death to temper their blade. Even with a hundred deaths, they've resolved to pierce through Kephale's body!"

Stelle nods grimly. It seems they all understand the danger. Even so, Mydei suspects he’s the only one who understands what must be done to stop it.

He scoffs. "All their honor is gone. How did the god of our tribe fall so low?" Nikador roars, but he ignores the noise and turns to Phainon instead. "Deliverer, here is your moment. I'll hold them off here and keep them from wielding the Blade of Fury. You need to head back and notify the two demigods."

As expected, his rival doesn’t respond well to his order. "Are you out of your mind, facing the Titan alone?! I'm staying, too.” He turns to their other ally, hand over his heart beseechingly. “Stelle, please—"

“Get lost!” Mydei roars. "Do you have to make me say this?"

Perhaps Stelle will not pick up on his meaning, but he is certain Phainon will. The other man knows how he feels about discussing his curse of immortality. Surely, Mydei does not have to lay out the obvious: he can be killed, and Phainon cannot.

The expression on Phainon’s face and his slightly parted lips suggests that even now, he intends to argue. Stubborn fool. Mydei changes tactics. He turns his back to the others and approaches the titan, speaking in a slightly calmer tone as he does."I must stay here, not for Okhema's safety, but to settle the score with my god. Even if immortality is a curse, it shouldn't be used so despicably."

It is the correct move. His fellow Chrysos Heir makes an audible noise of understanding. For all his flaws, Phainon understands honor. Perhaps more than that, he understands vengeance .

He adds, "Go, Deliverer. Your battlefield lies elsewhere."

Even turned away from Phainon, he can feel the weight of the man’s gaze. Something unspoken hangs between them.

"...Stay strong. Try not to get killed too many times."

The sound of retreating footsteps echoes as his two companions leave hastily. If all goes well, they will make it to Okhema with enough time to warn Aglaea and Tribbie of Nikador’s plan. If anyone can protect that city from the Strife Titan’s attack, it will be them.

"Finally, some peace," Mydei says, well aware that the others can still hear him. His words are, at least in part, for their benefit. They should leave this place knowing he is prepared for the fight ahead. "You and I—two warriors rejected by death. Is there any contest more fair than this?"

Mydei gazes once more upon his god. This time, the sight fills him with profound disgust. Once, Nikador’s mighty form left him in awe, made him proud to follow the most powerful of the titans. Now, the immortal mechanical being repulses him.

"Come forth! The king who has never claimed his throne, against the god who has fallen from grace. How perfectly matched we are!" He grins fiercely, staring directly into the empty face of Nikador. "Let's battle till the world's final breath!"

There is little room for thought when battling a god, at least a god as powerful as the Titan of Strife. There is only instinct. Nikador does not hesitate, does notslowly ramp up their attacks. They immediately heave their lance at Mydei. He evades the blade narrowly thanks to his battle-honed reflexes.The titan’s weapon shatters the stone floor where he’d just been standing as he scrambles from the spot.

“Not bad,” Mydei grins, drawing his own spear. “Finally, an actual challenge.”

His body twists and dodges and lunges faster than his conscious mind can work. They are evenly matched, both struggling to land a blow. It’s exhilarating to face a titan in one-on-one combat and be able to keep up. Despite the seriousness of the situation, he finds himself smiling. He’s having fun .

The stalemate continues. Mydei rolls, deflects, punches, and runs, seeking any opening he might find. Gradually, his body slows, tiring from the endless battle. He is fighting much more defensively than he normally would, but even this drains him. If only he can land a fatal blow, he might buy himself a minute or two to recuperate.

Finally, Mydei senses his opportunity. He jumps back as Nikador sweeps their lance in a giant arc. It tears against the stone floor of the arena, spewing fire in its wake. Before the flames can recede, he rushes to take advantage of the opening. Searing heat burns his feet but he ignores the pain and leaps forward, spear in hand. With all the strength he can summon, he thrusts the weapon into the titan.

His blade sings as it slides smoothly into Nikador's metal chest. It pierces the place the titan's heart would be, had they possessed one.

The monstrous creation stumbles back and lets out a pained, vicious cry. Mydei roars his own cry of victory in response. Adrenaline pulses through his veins as he drives his weapon deeper into the god’s wound. This is the glory of battle. It is blood, ashes, and the thrum of power running through his body. Few who are not Kremnoans truly comprehend this majesty of strife. To Mydei, nothing in this world is simpler.Honor and glory emerge when fear transforms into the will to fight, to protect.

Once again, the titan’s body falters and crumbles. Mydei wrenches his spear free of the pile, breathing heavily from the exertion of the kill. Even as he silently celebrates his victory over Nikador, he assesses the state of his own body. He’s bleeding from several wounds he hadn’t even noticed, and his limbs are starting to feel heavier from tiredness. He knows he’s already healing, and that his stamina is slowly replenishing, but he’s also aware that his limited self-regeneration abilities cannot possibly keep up with the pace of this combat. How long can he fight?

He has less time to savor the titan’s defeat than he anticipates. After only a minute or so, Nikador glows gold and reassembles once more. Though Mydei never truly let his guard down, he is still startled by how quickly the god manages to raise their blade and attack.

Mydei dodges the lance at the last second. For a brief moment, he thinks he’s managed to escape. Then, he’s hit with unbelievable pain like nothing he’s ever felt before as the tip tears into his side.

It’s like being crushed by the full weight of Georios’ mountain or the force of Phagousa’s sea. He’s thrown back, landing so hard all the breath is knocked from his lungs. His body scrapes excruciatingly across the floor of their arena before he comes to a stop. The gash in his torso is agonizing. When his hand finds the wound, he grimaces at the gory mess of rent flesh. He can feel his own blood soaking his pants and cooling.

There is no time to waste. He must move, before the titan has the chance to attack once again. But without air, his body struggles to respond. He’s almost managed to roll over when he hears Nikador’s cry of victory. He looks up just in time to seethe god’s lance run him through.

All goes dark.

This was not the first time Mydei had rushed to his death.

He's well aware that the people of Okhema, sheltered as they are by their sleeping titan, find the very idea barbaric. Even now, they look on the Kremnoans in their city with distrust, fearful of anyone who charges gladly into battle. In contrast, the descendants of Castor Kremnos understand that they face their possible demise every time they draw weapons, and eagerly embrace the risk.

For Mydei, though, the certainty with which he accepts his body’s destruction is unmatched even among his people. How could it not be? His father’s acts had unintentionally ensured that death would inevitably find him, and yet eternally evade him.

This is not the time to think of of death, of patricide and betrayed duty. Yet in the darkness, they are the only thoughts that come. Mydei remembers the outrage and horror on his father’s face as he impaled him on his spear. The blood—his blood, the blood of his ancestors—had gushed hot and thick over his arms. The iron tang had been nauseating, intoxicating. It reminded him of the tales of ancient Kremnoans, drinking the blood of defeated enemies. He’d had to stop himself from laughing in front of his warriors at the thought this is nothing like pomegranate juice . And then there was his advisor, urging him to take his rightful throne in this decaying fortress. No matter what the man said, Mydei remained steadfast. The blood of his father still clung to him, sticky as it dried and reeking of death.

Mydei opens his eyes.

The blood is his own, pooling around his still body. The death is his own, too. A false death. He balances a hand on the stone and pushes himself to a crouching position. His hand finds his discarded spear, and he rises to his full height once again.

“You won’t be rid of me that easily,” he laughs. After all, there is no audience now, just the mad god facing him, his distorted reflection. “I said we would battle til the end of the world, if that’s what it takes!”

Nearly every inch of him is covered in wounds. There are slashes from Nikador’s blade and flying debris. Abrasions mar his elbows and back from where he had skidded across the arena floor. The hole in his side is slowly closing, but the blood flow hasn’t quite stopped yet. No matter. He hefts his spear and surges forward as steadily as he can.

After their deaths, their fight grows more desperate.

The joy of their earlier battle evaporates. Where before they were evenly matched and rarely landed a hit, now both are wounded and opportunistic. When he blocks Nikador’s lance, the bones in his arms seem to grind together, and his muscles cry out in pain. Every punch that he lands on the titan reminds him of the state of his hands—skeleton and sinew decimated from the force of attacking a steel god.

Nikador falls at his hands twice more before Mydei makes another major mistake. This time, the sweeping lance attack takes him by surprise. He’s pummeled by the blade and engulfed in flames.

He dies.

He opens his eyes once more to that same cursed battlefield. Hecannot die.

He kills.

Every fiber of his being screams in agony. Every part feels like it has been destroyed, and is slowly reassembling, coming together inelegantly as the titan before him. His body seems like it is not his own. It is a prison he cannot escape.

Mydei loses all sense of time. The battle might have gone on for minutes, or hours, or perhaps even days. In the perpetual darkness of the evernight, it’s nearly impossible to tell. There are only the constants of exertion and steel ringing against steel.

He screams until his throat is shredded and he cannot make a sound. But the vocal cords start to mend, and his cries once more echo across the battlefield. Even when he cannot speak, there is the eternal clamor of blades and Nikador’s war cry, a sound chilling enough to reduce most mortals to terror.

His clothing is stained and the floor is slick with his own golden blood. No matter; his body keeps producing it, to make up for what he’s lost. He can’t die. He can’t escape. The smell makes his stomach turn.

When Nikador falls, he spares a second to wonder about the others. Did they make it back to Okhema? Is the city safe?

Where are they?

… did Phainon truly abandon him here?

It’s been so long—days, it must’ve been. Weeks. Why is it taking them so long to find a way tocounter Nikador’s immortal form?

Unless there is no solution. Unless he is meant to fight the titan forever, as he promised.

He is capable. This proves he is. He can fight for an eternity.

When he dies, his eyes fall shut for a few merciful moments. Calm, still darkness surrounds him, and the ache in his body subsides. Then, his eyes snap open again. He must fight. The world depends on it. His curse, his title, his destiny demands it.

He’s witnessed Castorice guiding souls to death. He’s seen how the overwhelming fear fades, how their eyelids slip shut and their lips slowly curl up to form a peaceful smile. Are mortals wrong to fear death, in the end? Perhaps death is the ultimate bliss, or at least the ultimate relief.

It’s the thing he will always be denied.

Release is not an option. His only choice is rage.

Anger surges through him just as hot and heady as the golden blood of a Chrysos Heir. Sorrow and regrets and bitterness blend in, too, but he feels mostly rage. His god is the cause of his every problem. The ruin of his family, his people, his life… all suffering wrought by the titan before him. He’s disgusted by them, this pathetic war god so frightened of death and defeat that they would become an immortal abomination.

So he fights. He fights on and on, his hatred and anger powering him no matter how many times he falls.

Pain, death, rage, war, Nikador’s battle cry, blood, death, resurrection, combat, agony, endless battle…

Maybe this is destiny. From the moment of his birth—before, even— everything has pointed to this. The Sea of Souls, the curse… his transformation into the perfect weapon to fight Nikador. A whole existence of strife to face Strife. Their fates intertwined, one and the same.

Madness for madness.

At some point, a red fog had crept in, unnoticed. He clings to rage to fend off the despair and madness. It is his greatest weapon. He must become the weapon. Rage is the weapon and so is he and he is rage...

—dei

The noise doesn’t register. The battlefield is full of noise; he hardly notices any of it now. He runs at Nikador once more, landing a solid hit against his leg.

Mydei

This time, he hears the sound, and pauses for a split second. There is something familiar about it. But it doesn’t come from the titan, so it is not important. He leaps into the air and scales the mechanical god. When he reaches the shoulder, he jumps and punches the titan’s headpiece. They toss him to the ground with a roar. It feels like his kneecap shatter on impact.

“Mydei!”

It’s a voice. A human voice. He turns his head toward the unexpected sound. Two figures run toward him, weapons drawn. One looks vaguely familiar, with short dark hair and strange clothes, and the other…

“Phainon?” he whispers. His voice sounds wrecked. The red fog recedes.

“Fuck, you’re…” He meets the man’s intense blue gaze, and feels something new. Relief. “Mydei, watch out!”

Mydei. Oh, right—that’s his name. His vision clears a bit more.

Thankfully, the other man—Dan Heng, he remembers now—is impressively fast, and manages to block the titan’s blade from plunging into Mydei’s heart.

“Thanks,” he says, clambering to his feet despite the ruined knee. It will fix itself soon. “Now let’s kill this thing!”

The titan, clearly unprepared for their onslaught, falls to their coordinated attacks. This time, Dan Heng lands the final blow, his spear hitting so hard that Nikador’s body fractures under it.

The temporary death of the titan gives them a moment to regroup.

Phainon wastes no time. “Mydei, you look…” He shakes his head. “Never mind. To make a long story short, Stelle and Castorice are researching how to break Nikador’s immortality. Dan Heng and I are here to help you fight.”

“Reinforcements, huh?” Mydei rolls his shoulder. It still feels wrecked, but he thinks he can swing his fist with it. “Well, thank you. But it wasn’t really necessary. I was managing on my own.”

“Ha! I bet you were!”

“I do appreciate it, though. Just… try to stay back. Believe me when I say that even a single hit from the titan can kill.”

Dan Heng speaks up. “We’ll take up the rear. We should all focus on fighting defensively. There’s not much else we can do until the others find out how to strip away Nikador’s immortality.”

“Good idea,” Phainon nods. “We’ll avoid taking any major damage and make sure we keep them occupied.” He elbows Mydei lightly. “That includes you, too, my friend.”

“Hmph, we’ll see about that.” Mydei grasps his spear and aims it at his god’s towering form. “I’m determined to face this thing to the end. No matter what it costs.”

Chapter Notes

Chapter 2 is up! Please note the rating change as this fic now contains a lot of smut!

I was rushing to get this out before 3.1 drops since the patch will probably ruin all my attempts at making the story canon-compliant. Please note the new tags and enjoy!

The moment they return to Okhema, Mydei informs the others that he's going to rest. Their expressions range from curious to deeply concerned. Mydei turns to the city to avoid them.

"Rest up, De! Feel better soon!" says Tribbie. Despite their typical childish enthusiasm, the demigod sounds exhausted. He wonders how much operating the Century Gate took out of them.

"Mydei, are you…?” It's Phainon, of course. "I've never seen you look so —"

After everything today, he’s far too drained for the other man’s questions. "I'm going now," Mydei declares. Before anyone can object, he walks away from the group, down the path deeper into the city.

He goes quickly, without looking back, though the weight of their stares falls on him heavily. It's clear there's more to discuss—the fate of the Coreflame, what the fragment of Nikador had told Castorice and Stelle, and what comes next—but they won't need him for any of it. They'll be fine without him now that the battle is over.

Even so, departing like this feels vaguely shameful. It's an admission he's reached his limit. He knows they wouldn’t look down on him for his injuries; they’re all too kind for that. But he’s so accustomed to leading the

Kremnoans that he avoids showing such weakness at all costs. He does the same now, walking away as briskly as he can, minimizing his limp to be as imperceptible as possible. Some Okhemans notice him, as they always do— neither his hair nor attire allow him to blend in—but judging by the reactions he earns, he must not look like he’s died countless times today.

Normally, the long walk across the cityis entirely unremarkable to him. Today, however, Mydei finds himself reflecting on Okhema. Perhaps it’s because his battered body feels every step of the journey; or maybe it’s because he’d just visited Castrum Kremnos for the first time in twenty years. That fortress had never truly been his home, not like it was for most Kremnoans. His father had made sure of that. But it was still the closest thing he’d had to a place he’d belonged.

Despite—or perhaps because of—his history, he’d walked its ruined paths and silent halls with clear eyes. Castrum Kremnos had once been a monument to power and human determination, always ringing with the sounds of colossal engineering projects and relentless combat. The other city states had lived in fear of its might for eons. Yet in the end, it had been lost to crazed plots and reduced to rubble so quickly. The fortress is now merely an empty husk of its former glory.

Would his people, so long in exile, still desire to return there? Or is Kremnos truly gone?

Where Castrum Kremnos had been like a tomb, dead and decaying and haunted by the undying, Okhema is startlingly alive. The streets are crowded with people and dromases, the sounds of their voices and labor creating a bustling atmosphere. The towering marble buildings glow in the perpetual sunlight, and lush plants grow eagerly toward Kephale. It’s all so mundane, yet so wondrous: an entire city living as though the black tide had never descended.

He’d hated it here when he arrived. The Okheman people seemed so passive and spoiled, their city among the cloudslavish and impractical. Mydei had led the exiled Kremnoan detachment here because it was the only place that might accept them, but their relationship has always been an uneasy one. There are still many Okhemans who see his people as

bloodthirsty savages who would betray their neighbors at the earliest opportunity.

The Kremnoans have their own lingering prejudices, believing Okhemans to be cowardly, dishonorable, weak, and foolish. In the face of the apocalypse, all they’d done was put their faith in Kephale and the Chrysos Heirs. To a child of Kremnos, such inaction in the face of an invasion was pathetic, idiotic, infuriating .

Yet Okhema stands untouched and untroubled, while Castrum Kremnos is a ruin and Nikador is dead.

It strikes Mydei that he's lived in Okhema for more years than all those he’d spent in Castrum Kremnos. These streets are now more familiar to him than those of his homeland, its people no longer strangers. Other Kremnoans wave and call out to him, but so do some Okhemans, and he has to put up his hand to wave some away.

Upon leaving Castrum Kremnos, he’d felt no loss or regrets. Rather, when he opened his eyes on this city, he’d felt himself relax ever-so-slightly. Could it be that after so long, he's unwittingly come to feel at peace here?

By the time he arrives at the Marmoreal Palace, Mydei’s reserve of energy has drained to the final dregs. He’s no longer able to completely hide his limp, his injured knee too painful and wrecked from pushing himself. Fortunately, he knows the back passages of this place well. Once he slips into the darker, hidden halls, he can slow his pace and hobble without worrying about being spotted. A warrior prince in such a state would likely send a panic through not only the Okhemans, but also his own people. He’d rather avoid causing such a stir.

His rooms are at the top floor of the baths, high above the streets. Aglaea had offered the suite to him years ago, on account of him being a Chrysos heir. It feels a bit too much like charity for his liking, but his advisor Krateros had begged him to accept it. The older man had a point: this space is far more befitting a crown prince than the massively overpriced apartments he'd been renting in the city before. The role of deserter prince living in exile paid far less than Okhemans assumed. Even if he'd been

dishonorable enough to make off with the treasures of Castrum Kremnos, it wouldn't have made much difference: his father had already squandered most of their fortune on his schemes. However, this meant nothing in the eternal holy city. Most landlords took a look at Mydei and proclaimed that their vacancies had recently become occupied. The only ones that would rent to him were those who quoted clearly extortionate rates.

At last, Mydei slips into his rooms unnoticed. After living in them for years, they’ve started to feel like they’re his, despite their Okheman aesthetics. He's not sure he'll ever get used to the wholly unnecessary luxuries: delicate and lustrous fabrics, the window made of colored glass in intricate patterns, the ornate mosaic tub, and tables heaped with fresh fruits and wine. And of course there is the eternal sun, ever bright and unchanging.

Once, that sun had kept him awake at all hours, though he’d been too stubborn to admit it. Now, however, he is used to its presence. Besides, he’s far too exhausted for the light to bother him. Mydei strips out of his filthy clothes and sinks into the hot water of his private bath. The heat immediately relaxes his muscles and helps ease his excruciating pain. He scrubs off the lingering blood and muck that he had been unable to remove back at Castrum Kremnos. Before long, he feels his eyelids slide shut, and slips into an irresistible sleep.

A loud knock rouses him from his rest some time later.

Mydei feels like he’s been trampled by an entire group of dromases, repeatedly. His whole body aches, muscles and bones and skin alike all protesting the stress he’d put them through.

There’s another knock, then someone shouting, “Mydei? Are you alright?”

He recognizes that voice. With a groan, he realizes that Phainon is probably attracting all sorts of unwanted attention with his yelling. Mydei shifts his body into a more upright position and calls out, “Come in.”

A thick mane of silver hair pokes into the room first, as though he’s checking for a trap. Phainon wears a surprised expression as he enters and

lets the heavy doors close behind him. “I was starting to doubt that you would invite me in.”

Mydei crosses his arms. “You were making a scene out there.”

“Well, I wouldn’t have had to yell if you’d just answered me!” Despite his protest, Phainon’s lips turn up to a sunny smile.

It makes Mydei roll his eyes. How is the other man so happy and energetic after everything? “I was sleeping, Deliverer.”

That makes Phainon squint. “But you’re in the bath.” When Mydei doesn’t reply, he continues, “You can’t just sleep in the bath! What if you… I don’t know, fall over?”

“Are you worried I’m going to drown and die?”

“Okay, fair enough.” Phainon says.

His guest falls quiet after that. It’s somewhat unsettling—in his experience, Phainon never shuts up—so Mydei decides to break the awkward silence. “Is there some reason you’re here?”

Phainon gives him a look, like he thinks Mydei might be an idiot. “I wanted to make sure my friend is doing okay, obviously.”

“We’re not friends.”

The second he says it, Mydei regrets his words. He hadn’t meant for them to sound so… harsh.

“Do you really have to treat me like an enemy? Even after today?”

Phainon’s face seems transformed from his usual cheer, and his voice sounds hurt. Even from this distance, the dark circles under his eyes and his grim expression make him look thoroughly exhausted. While he hadn’t fought Nikador for quite as long, Phainon had been running himself ragged, too.

Unbidden, Mydei remembers the relief he’d felt when Phainon had arrived and interrupted his unending duel with Nikador. If the other man hadn’t arrived, he’s not sure he would’ve emerged from that conflict with his sanity intact.

Apologies have never been his strong suit, though. Instead, Mydei says, “You don’t need to stand over there. You can join me.”

Phainon raises his eyebrows in surprise, yet he doesn’t say anything as he strips out of his clothing and clambers into the pool. He chooses a spot next to Mydei, on one of the ledges that double as steps and seats. It’s about halfway down the bath, deep enough to cover him to the waist. The position leaves Phainon close enough to touch, but not in his personal space. Mydei doesn’t mind it too much.
